body_markdown:
The legendary[chase scene in Bullitt](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hq8YD7-Aimw) was filmed using German newsreel cameras that weighed approximately 30 pounds and shot 24 frames per second. If you happen to be reading this on an iPhone made in the past decade or an equivalent Android, you are holding a half-pound camera capable of shooting at 60 frames per second. So if you want to take and share compelling videos of your cars, you already have the gear—you just have to know how to use it. Let[Isaac Shapiro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/ishapirohagerty-com/) , whose full-time job is to create videos for Hagerty’s social media channels, be your guide.


*Welcome to the[Hagerty Movies and Cars Celebration](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine-features/welcome-to-the-hagerty-movies-and-cars-celebration/) , where we highlight and explore the relationship between[cars and the silver screen](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/movies-and-cars/) .*


## Take the Compromises out of Your Camera


**Get Set Up Like a Pro:** Your phone’s default settings compromise quality for space and control for ease of use. Let’s change that.


Unsplash/Nejc Soklič


“The iPhone does a lot of things for you that it thinks are correct when in reality it’s making it worse,” Shapiro says. The phone’s default settings strike a compromise between quality, ease of use, and preserving hard drive space—which are fine for recording your grandkids opening a birthday present but fall short of what’s needed for high-level car cinematography.


Shapiro’s specific recommendations quickly get into the technical weeds (see the video below for step-by-step instructions), but they have three simple goals: increase the quality of the recording, give you more control, and make the video look more “natural” and less, well, like it was shot on a phone.


[https://cdn.emagazines.com/default/CarCinematography-GePro_afe82f6e-1bd2-4274-9265-32a1a9b4bf23.mp4](https://cdn.emagazines.com/default/CarCinematography-GePro_afe82f6e-1bd2-4274-9265-32a1a9b4bf23.mp4)


Here’s what Shapiro adjusts (again, follow along with the video above to do it yourself).


- **Aspect Ratio** – The proportions of the video or, even more simply, how you hold your phone. Think about where you intend for your video to be watched—probably on the phones of your friends and family, which are usually held vertically, not on your 80-inch flat-screen television (horizontal).
- **Formats** – How you want the video saved. The phone defaults to a space-saving format. Setting it to “most compatible” allows for a larger, but higher-quality, file.
- **Record Video** – Here you’re setting resolution and frame rate. In simpler terms, how much detail do you want to record? Shapiro goes for 4K (2160 x 3840) resolution, 60 frames per second—which is equivalent to an ultra-high-resolution Blu-ray disc. Note: This will take up considerable space on your phone.
- **Auto Adjustments** – Shut off several “auto” features, including HDR and Auto FPS.
- **Macro Control** – Many phones have a second “macro” lens for capturing objects up close. This setting lets you, rather than the phone, decide when to use it.
- **Grid & Level** – Fills your screen with a grid and level, which can help you make sure cars are aligned properly.
- **Exposure -0.3 to -0.7** – The iPhone camera’s default exposure is very bright, which can improperly render darker car colors and generally make things look artificial. Shapiro compensates by telling the phone to “underexpose.”


## Don’t Just Stand There!


Now the camera is set up correctly, but you need to know where and how to point it. Subtle tweaks in how you frame a shot can dramatically improve it. Hagerty’s social channels have developed a visual language all their own, yet Shapiro’s advice for capturing footage essentially stresses cinematography fundamentals. See if you can identify some of his recommended shots (exemplified in the video below) in your favorite movies. The overall goal, he says, is movement. “Dynamic shots are king. Don’t just stand there and swivel the camera.”


[https://cdn.emagazines.com/default/CarCinematography-It%27sClutter_f9dd73ae-0580-4185-9b5b-12913f9a25b9.mp4](https://cdn.emagazines.com/default/CarCinematography-It%27sClutter_f9dd73ae-0580-4185-9b5b-12913f9a25b9.mp4)


- **Parallax** – Foreground and background are moving at different speeds. Adds visual interest.
- **Dolly** – Replicates a wheeled platform moving toward or away from the subject.
- **Match** – Two shots that look similar save for one detail.
- **Tilt** – Angling the camera creatively can add depth to your scene.
- **Reveal** – Open with your camera purposely blocked by something—a wall, another car, a tree, etc.—and then slowly show your subject.
- **Through** – Shoot through another object (e.g., a detail of another car) onto your subject.


Many of these shots run against what we think of as “clean” composition. The people and stuff standing between you and the subject aren’t clutter—they’re what makes the video interesting. “Clean shots are boring,” Shapiro says.


## The Cutting Room Floor


Any director can tell you that movies are really made in the editing room. This is where you trim out boring footage, crop to focus on key details, and stitch together multiple videos into one movie. It’s also where you can compress the video (i.e., pare down the resolution and/or frame rate) so that it can be easily shared. Now, you may be thinking, “Why did I go through the trouble of recording a high-quality video only to shrink it back down?” The answer, again, comes down to control: Starting with a big, rich video allows you to choose what to remove.


Most editing can be done on the phone. Two popular applications are CapCut and Edits, respectively associated with TikTok and Instagram. They’re useful even if you’re not planning to post on those platforms (of course they both have ways of encouraging you to do just that).


## Extras


Your phone alone and a steady hand will serve you well. But we all love gadgets. The most useful is a gimbal, which will stabilize your shot. Wireless microphones can help improve audio quality, particularly if you want certain sounds and voices to be heard above the din (e.g., if you’d like to interview someone at a racetrack). Shapiro recommends these, but there are plenty of options out there.


**Osmo Mobile 7P:** A simple gimbal and tripod for your phone that retails for about $100.


DJI


**DJI Mic 2:** Small wireless microphones that easily clip on people. About $200 with charging case.


DJI


## Make It Yours


The most powerful piece of equipment on you is neither your phone nor whatever gizmo you’ve attached to it—it’s what’s between your ears. What are you trying to communicate? “Envision the final product while you’re shooting,” Shapiro advises. He acknowledges doing so isn’t easy. Start by becoming a student of the videos that attract you. “Is the video interesting? Why are you watching it? Apply that to your own stuff,” he says.
